cash.usd: Accepted by many safari operators, tour companies and larger hotels, which often quote in dollars. Day to day (shops, matatus, markets) you need shillings or M-Pesa.
cash.atms: Common in towns and cities, inside banks, malls and supermarkets. Most accept foreign Visa and Mastercard cards; your own bank may charge a fee on top.
cash.cards: Accepted in malls, supermarkets, chain restaurants and mid-range or better hotels. Small shops, kiosks and matatus are cash or M-Pesa only.
cash.exchange: Banks and licensed forex bureaus in city centres, malls and at the airport. Bureaus usually beat airport rates; bring your passport.
cash.refusedUSD: It is commonly reported that US dollar notes printed before ~2006 (some places say ~2009), small notes, and torn, marked or written-on notes are refused or get a worse rate. Bring clean, recent $50 and $100 notes for the best rate.
cash.verify: Confirm the cut-off year bureaus currently apply to older US dollar notes.

fxNotes.title: Official and parallel rates differ
fxNotes.body: Burundi has had a large gap between the official exchange rate and the parallel (street) rate, at times the street rate offering roughly twice as many francs per dollar. Changing money outside licensed banks and bureaus is illegal and risky. The central bank has taken steps to narrow the gap, so check the current situation before you travel.
fxNotes.verify: Check the current official rate, the size of the parallel gap and any recent changes by the BRB.

cash.atms: Common in Addis Ababa and larger towns; many accept foreign Visa cards, Mastercard less reliably. Daily limits can be low.

fxNotes.title: The birr was floated in 2024
fxNotes.body: In July 2024 Ethiopia let the birr move to a market-based rate, and it lost more than half its value against the US dollar within months. Before that, the street rate was roughly double the official one; since the float the gap has narrowed a lot. Prices in birr have risen with it, so older guidebook prices are out of date. Use banks or licensed bureaus.
fxNotes.verify: Check the current official rate and whether any meaningful parallel-market gap remains.

fxNotes.title: Fast-moving rate with an official/parallel gap

fxNotes.title: A dollarised economy with unreliable shilling notes
fxNotes.body: Somalia runs largely on US dollars and mobile money. Shilling notes are mostly old, worn and many are counterfeit, so they trade at street rates and are only used for small purchases. The Central Bank of Somalia has announced plans for new notes; check whether they have arrived.
fxNotes.verify: Check the status of the Central Bank of Somalia's currency reform and new notes.

fxNotes.title: Fixed official rate, strict currency rules
fxNotes.body: The nakfa is officially fixed at 15 to the US dollar, while the street rate is widely reported to be much weaker. Changing money outside official channels is illegal and penalties can be serious. Visitors are generally required to declare foreign currency on arrival and to keep exchange receipts, and holding foreign currency inside the country is tightly controlled.
fxNotes.verify: Check current declaration rules, limits on foreign currency and how visitors are expected to pay.
